title: Capturing and piece values
objectives: Understand that capturing means removing an opponent's piece by moving onto its square
Know the rough relative value of each piece

steps.text: To capture, move your piece onto the square an enemy piece occupies, following that piece's own movement rules. The enemy piece is removed from the board.
Pieces aren't all equal. A rough guide: pawn = 1, knight = 3, bishop = 3, rook = 5, queen = 9. The king is priceless — losing him ends the game.

steps.prompt: Capture the black knight on d5 with your queen.

hints.text: The queen captures the same way she moves — in a straight line or a diagonal, landing exactly on the enemy piece's square.
The knight is one square diagonally from your queen.
Move the queen here to capture.
The queen captures on d5 — one diagonal step from e4.

feedback.default: That move doesn't land the queen exactly on d5, where the knight is. A capture only works if you move onto the enemy piece's own square.

steps.successExplanation: Qxd5 captures the knight. The queen moves diagonally from e4 to d5, landing exactly on the square the knight occupied.

steps.prompt: Which trade is roughly equal in value?
options: Trading your queen for a pawn
Trading your knight for a rook
Trading your bishop for a knight
Trading your rook for a pawn

feedback.0: A queen (worth about 9) for a pawn (worth about 1) is a huge loss — nowhere close to equal.
feedback.1: A knight (about 3) for a rook (about 5) actually favors you — you'd be gaining value, not trading evenly.
feedback.3: A rook (about 5) for a pawn (about 1) is a big loss of value for you.

steps.successExplanation: Right — a bishop and a knight are both worth about 3 points, so trading one for the other is roughly even.
